item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 835 as four die in 24 hours
item.description:
Four more children died with measles-like symptoms in 24 hours until 8:00am on Thursday, bringing the combined tally of confirmed and suspected measles-related deaths to 835 in the country.
According to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), all the latest fatalities were suspected measles deaths.
With the latest update, the number of suspected measles deaths has risen to 739, while the number of laboratory-confirmed measles deaths remained 96.
A total of 870 new suspected measles cases were reported during the 24-hour period, bringing the cumulative number of suspected cases nationwide to 127,410.
Meanwhile, 135 new confirmed measles cases were recorded, bringing the total number of laboratory-confirmed infections to 15,874.
Since March 15, a total of 110,182 patients with suspected measles have been hospitalised across the country, of whom 106, 053 have recovered, according to DGHS data.

item.title: Fakhrul: PM raises hopes for social change in post-July Bangladesh
item.description:
Local Government, Rural Development (LGRD) and Cooperatives Minister Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on Thursday said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is raising hopes for social change in post-July Bangladesh by promoting behavioral change and efforts to build a non-communal society.
He made the remarks while addressing a publication unveiling ceremony, photography exhibition, and discussion at the Department of Films and Publications (DFP) Auditorium, organized to mark July Martyrs' Day 2026.
Fakhrul, who also serves as secretary general of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), said the prime minister has urged people to dispose of waste in dustbins and instructed city corporations to maintain cleaner cities.
He said the prime minister is inspiring young people and trying to change social behavior to build a new Bangladesh.
The minister said it would be difficult to move the country forward without changing public attitudes. He also said there has been no visible progress in implementing the aspirations of the July Uprising over the past 5 months.
He said: "Only the prime minister is holding the change to build the country and society. Many who used to take bribes, commit corruption, and exploit opportunities are changing their stance from fascists to take advantage of the July changes. All this is sad."
He added that the prime minister is working to change those practices.
Referring to Bangladesh's political history, Fakhrul said people have repeatedly sacrificed their lives since 1947 in pursuit of social change but the goal of establishing an inequality-free society has remained unfulfilled.
He said many people sacrificed their lives between 1952 and 2024 in efforts to transform society.
He said: "Pakistan was divided, and Bangladesh was led by leaders like Maulana Bhashani and AK Fazlul Haque, but the society did not change. After 1971, the fascist ruler was ousted in 2024 at the cost of countless lives."
The minister also stressed the need to change consumerist behavior to uphold the spirit of July.
He said: "The chair of power is very strange. Sitting in the chair of power creates a different feeling. The chemistry changes after coming to power. The youth of 2024 have demanded a change in the character of the chair of power."
Fakhrul said he had often questioned where the youth who would change the country were, adding that young people came forward during the 2024 movement and helped oust what he described as a fascist regime.
He said: "If we go back to that previous society, the sacrifice of hundreds of lives will go in vain. We should value those who sacrificed their lives."
The BNP leader also referred to former prime minister Begum Khaleda Zia, describing her as the country's first female freedom fighter.
He said that after Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman declared independence, Khaleda Zia told soldiers: "All the orders of your commander are final. The call for independence must be followed."
Fakhrul said Khaleda Zia was imprisoned and continued to struggle for the people throughout her life. He added that after Sheikh Hasina left the country, Khaleda Zia, despite serious illness, called in a video message for building a Bangladesh free from revenge.
Information and Broadcasting Minister Zahir Uddin Swapon chaired the event. Among those present were State Minister for Information Yasser Khan Choudhury, Public Service Commission (PSC) member Dr Chowdhury Saima Ferdous, senior officials of the ministry and its affiliated organizations, media personnel, and invited guests.
The guests also unveiled a July Martyrs' Day publication and visited a photography exhibition at the venue.

item.title: Mahdi: Malaysia to resume hiring Bangladeshi workers from late August
item.description:
Malaysia will resume recruitment of Bangladeshi workers from the last week of August, Prime Minister’s Adviser and spokesperson Mahdi Amin said on Thursday.
“We have set a realistic target so that Bangladeshi workers can start travelling to Malaysia from the last week of August,” he said at a press conference at the Bangladesh High Commission in Kuala Lumpur.
Labour and Employment and Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury was also present at the press conference.
Mahdi thanked the Malaysian government for taking steps to reopen the labour market after a prolonged suspension, expressing gratitude to Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, Human Resources Minister Datuk Seri R. Ramanan and other relevant authorities for their cooperation.
He said the government’s efforts have been guided by the principle of “Bangladesh First” to protect the interests of the country’s large workforce, expressing hope that the resumption of worker migration would make a significant contribution to Bangladesh’s economy in the long run.
Mahdi urged aspiring migrant workers to remain patient and follow official procedures, warning them against middlemen and fraudulent syndicates.
He said the government would take strict action against brokers and dishonest recruitment networks to ensure that workers are not subjected to harassment or exploitation.
The adviser said technical-level work between the two countries would begin shortly, with the Bangladesh High Commission in Kuala Lumpur and the Malaysian High Commission in Dhaka working jointly to facilitate the process.

item.title: Law minister: Hasina to face legal action if she returns to Bangladesh
item.description:
Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Md Asaduzzaman on Thursday said former prime minister and condemned convict Sheikh Hasina will face legal action in accordance with the law if she returns to Bangladesh.
He made the remarks while responding to questions from reporters at a ceremony for signing a Memorandum of Understanding between the National Legal Aid Services Organization and non-governmental organizations BRAC and BLAST on legal aid at the Secretariat.
Asked about a recent interview in which Hasina said she plans to return to Bangladesh in December, the law minister said the home ministry is making efforts for her extradition.
"If she comes, the law will take its own course. We will not do anything in violation of the law. We will exercise the authority that the law gives us," Asaduzzaman said.
Asked how Hasina could return as she does not have a passport, the minister said, "How she will come is her problem. It is not our problem."
"When she enters our jurisdiction, I will exercise the authority given to me by law and enforce the law. That's as simple as it is," he said.

item.title: Japan quake toll hits 34 as survivors struggle in heat
item.description:
Japanese emergency workers searched tirelessly for survivors at a wrecked shopping mall on Thursday, as the death toll from a major earthquake hit 34 and tens of thousands were left without power in punishing heat.
The Kumamoto disaster management office issued the new tally for Tuesday’s quake, with seven bodies now extracted from the mass of rubble, steel and wires of the Aeon shopping mall after a suspected gas blast.
Eight people were also confirmed dead at the Nippon Paper Industries factory in Yatsushiro city, where part of a red-and-white smokestack collapsed, according to the office.
Five others were in a critical condition after the 7.1-magnitude tremor, while almost 9,500 locals were in evacuation centers in the region of southwestern Japan on the island of Kyushu.
The quake caused widespread damage, flattening homes, damaging bridges, triggering fires and leaving tens of thousands of residents without power and water in temperatures forecast to hit 38C this weekend.
Some 13,520 households remained without electricity on Thursday.
Hundreds of elderly people -- Japan has the world’s second-oldest population -- slumbered on thin mats on the hard lobby floor at one community center in Uki city as they sought relief from the searing sun.
“Thank God for these shelters,” said one woman, who declined to give her name, as people slept between chairs and tables or gathered around a television.
At home or in the car “it’s too hot and there are too many mosquitoes,” she told AFP.
“In this heat, if you don’t have electricity and air conditioning, it’s very tough,” father-of-four supermarket employee Hiroyuki Matsushima, 53, told AFP.
With no power and running water, Retiree Kenji Ota, 72, has been sleeping inside his car at night.
“This quake was so strong. It was horrible... I can only sleep for two hours or so at night,” he said.
The town of Hikawa was one of the areas worst hit, where many older structures crumpled in the quake and where residents still had no water or power on Thursday.
“The biggest problem is that there is no toilet... I had to go to a nearby school,” said Kinuko Uemura, 85, who told AFP she and her husband were lucky to survive the collapse of their traditional house.
Soshiro Okawa, 59, was at the back of his roadside souvenir shop when the quake struck.
“It was my first time experiencing an earthquake that literally made the ground rise,” he said.
The 59-year-old heard items breaking inside his store while the ground swelled in the parking lot, shattering its asphalt surface and a series of cracks stretched into the foundation of his shop.
The store will suspend operations, but Okawa said that “we need to ensure the livelihood of our growers and job security for my staff.”
The Aeon shopping mall was evacuated after the earthquake but around 50 minutes later the facility was gutted by the massive blast with an unknown number of employees still inside.
Businessman Fumihiko Matsuura, 56, said he had watched the latest “Toy Story” movie at the mall only a week or so ago.
“I was here. I was just here,” he told AFP. “It’s like I narrowly escaped the danger.”
Footage from inside showed rescue workers in orange overalls and white helmets picking their way through a mass of twisted steel, dangling cables and chunks of ceiling.
A total of 25 felines from a “cat cafe” were however rescued, triggering widespread relief on social media.
TV footage showed people queueing for petrol and drinking water. Authorities have sent hundreds of air conditioning units to shelters.
The US Geological Survey measured the quake at 6.8, lower than Japan’s reading of 7.1.
Japan is one of the world’s most seismically active countries, sitting on top of four major tectonic plates along the western edge of the Pacific “Ring of Fire.”
Kumamoto itself was hit by two devastating earthquakes in 2016, which killed 273 people and injured more than 2,800.
The archipelago, home to around 125 million people, typically experiences hundreds of jolts every year and accounts for about 18 percent of the world’s earthquakes.
The vast majority are mild, although the damage they cause varies according to their location and the depth below the Earth’s surface at which they strike.
Japan is haunted by the memory of a massive 9.0-magnitude undersea quake in 2011, which triggered a tsunami that killed or left missing around 18,500 people and wrecked the Fukushima nuclear plant.

item.title: Myanmar repatriation would risk Rohingya lives
item.description:
Malaysia’s main Rohingya rights group urged the government on Thursday to halt the planned deportation of some 5,000 stateless asylum seekers to Myanmar, saying their lives would be at risk.
The appeal came a day after Malaysia’s Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Myanmar had agreed to take back 5,000 Rohingya, in a rare repatriation push announced days after authorities detained dozens of refugees.
Malaysia hosts more than 215,000 refugees and asylum seekers registered with the UN refugee agency, including more than 126,000 members of Myanmar’s persecuted Rohingya minority, making them the country’s largest refugee community.
The Myanmar Ethnic Rohingya Human Rights Organization in Malaysia asked Anwar and his home minister to consult the UN refugee agency and Rohingya representatives before any repatriation.
Sending Rohingya back to Myanmar would violate “the core international law principle of non-refoulement, which bans returning people to a place where their lives are threatened,” the rights group said in a statement.
“The Rohingya are stateless... There is no way we can return home safely when we face ongoing genocide back home,” it said.
“How can stateless Rohingya be safe in Myanmar?”
According to the statement, repatriated Rohingya could be forced to join the Myanmar military without training and be used as human shields in fighting with other ethnic groups.
The group also urged the international community to intervene without delay.
Malaysian authorities this week detained more than 100 Rohingya refugees who had gathered outside the UN refugee agency’s office in Kuala Lumpur after being threatened with eviction from an informal settlement in northern Penang state.
Officials later confirmed that the detainees had valid documentation issued by the UN agency.
The group was released on Wednesday and sent to various locations around Malaysia after undergoing final verification, local media reported.
Malaysia, which shelters one of Southeast Asia’s biggest refugee populations, is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention and does not formally recognize refugee status.
AFP fact-checkers have found that Rohingya refugees in Malaysia have been targeted by online disinformation campaigns that rights advocates say are fueling xenophobia and intimidation.
Many of the Rohingya, a mostly Muslim group, escaped Myanmar during a brutal military crackdown in 2017.

item.title: Sarjis Alam's car attacked in Sylhet's Golapganj
item.description:
A vehicle carrying National Citizen Party (NCP) Northern Region Chief Organizer Sarjis Alam came under attack in Sylhet's Golapganj on Thursday afternoon while returning from a party event.
The incident occurred around 2:45pm, according to police.
Golapganj Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Mohammad Sabed Ali said a 7-Up bottle was hurled at the microbus carrying Sarjis in Golapganj municipality, shattering its rear window.
"No one was injured in the incident. Efforts are underway to identify those involved," the OC said.
According to witnesses, Sarjis attended a program with the families of July uprising martyrs at the Golapganj Upazila Auditorium on Thursday morning. NCP leader Mahmuda Mitu also attended the event.
After the program, the leaders were heading to Hetimganj Bazar for lunch when the attack took place in front of Noor Mansion near the Golapganj Upazila gate.
Following the incident, the NCP leaders cancelled their lunch plan and left for the Sylhet Circuit House.
Witnesses also alleged that another attempt was made to attack the convoy in the bypass area shortly afterwards.
Police said members of the police, the Armed Police Battalion (APBn) and other law enforcement agencies were deployed in and around the Golapganj Upazila Parishad area following the incidents.
The NCP is scheduled to attend another program in Kanaighat later in the day.
Earlier this week, the party's July Padyatra program in Habiganj also came under attack. NCP leaders blamed Chhatra Dal for that incident. On Wednesday, the party alleged that its central leaders' convoy faced repeated police obstruction in Srimangal and Bahubal while travelling from Moulvibazar to Habiganj to attend a protest program.

item.title: When childhood becomes the first casualty of climate change
item.description:
There was a time when climate change in Bangladesh was discussed through the language of infrastructure. The conversation revolved around embankments, cyclone shelters, flood control projects, adaptation funds, and carbon emissions. Success was measured by the number of kilometres of embankments built or the amount of international climate finance secured. Children appeared in these discussions only as passive victims to be rescued after disaster struck.
The latest Children’s Climate Risk Report 2026 by Unicef demands that we abandon that habit of thinking. It suggests something far more unsettling. Bangladesh is not merely fighting a climate crisis. It is slowly becoming a place where childhood itself is being reshaped by an environment that is growing increasingly hostile.
This is perhaps the most important lesson hidden beneath the report’s alarming statistics. Climate change is no longer only about damaged roads, submerged villages or destroyed crops. It is altering what it means to grow up in Bangladesh.
The report places Bangladesh fourth among the countries where children face the highest climate risks, with an overall vulnerability score of 9.38 out of 10. Only Myanmar, Pakistan, and Vietnam rank higher. Bangladesh receives the maximum possible risk score, 10 out of 10, for riverine flooding, making its children the most exposed in the world to this particular hazard. The country’s scores remain alarmingly high across nearly every category, including tropical cyclones at 9.7, air pollution at 9.7, drought at 9.65, extreme heat at 9.24, and coastal flooding at 8.13.
These numbers are disturbing enough. Yet the real story lies in what they collectively reveal.
Climate disasters rarely arrive one at a time anymore. Bangladesh increasingly experiences overlapping emergencies where one hazard begins before another has fully disappeared. Floods are followed by disease outbreaks. Cyclones are followed by prolonged displacement. Heatwaves arrive before communities recover from previous disasters. Air pollution quietly intensifies throughout the year, affecting children even when skies appear clear.
The report captures this reality by arguing that Bangladeshi children are exposed not to isolated disasters but to multiple climate shocks simultaneously.
Nearly 60 million children in Bangladesh are exposed to at least one climate-related hazard. More than 24 million face the combined risks of floods, droughts, and cyclones. Around 32 million children are directly threatened by riverine flooding, about 22 million by cyclones, while roughly 60 million are exposed to drought and air pollution.
These figures are difficult to comprehend because they describe an entire generation rather than isolated communities.
The tendency is often to think of climate change through dramatic images of flooded villages or collapsing riverbanks. Those images matter, but they obscure a slower crisis unfolding inside classrooms, hospitals, and homes.
When schools become shelters after cyclones, education stops. When repeated flooding destroys family income, children become workers instead of students. When prolonged displacement breaks community networks, girls become more vulnerable to early marriage while boys face greater pressure to enter informal labour markets. Health deteriorates because clean drinking water becomes scarce, sanitation systems collapse and disease spreads more easily.
The damage extends well beyond the immediate disaster.
A child who misses several months of education today may experience lower earnings decades later. A malnourished infant exposed to repeated climate shocks may never fully recover physically or cognitively. Psychological trauma caused by repeated disasters often remains invisible, although it shapes behaviour and emotional well-being for years.
These are losses that no disaster compensation package can fully repair.
One of the most overlooked findings in the Unicef report is that Bangladesh actually performs comparatively better in several traditional child development indicators such as child health, nutrition, education, poverty reduction, and maternal mortality. In other words, the country has made genuine progress over the past decades.
Yet climate change threatens to reverse those achievements. The environmental conditions necessary to sustain these gains are becoming increasingly unstable. Development successes built over decades now stand on uncertain ecological foundations.
Perhaps this explains why conventional adaptation strategies increasingly appear insufficient.
Much of Bangladesh’s climate planning understandably focuses on physical infrastructure. Cyclone shelters save lives. Embankments reduce flood damage. River dredging improves water management. These remain essential investments.
However, the next stage of adaptation requires a different question. Instead of asking how infrastructure survives climate change, policy-makers must ask how childhood survives climate change.
These are not identical questions. Children experience disasters differently from adults because their bodies, minds, and futures are still developing. A week without school affects an eight-year-old differently than it affects a thirty-year-old office worker. Air pollution permanently damages developing lungs more severely than adult lungs. Malnutrition during childhood produces lifelong consequences that cannot simply be reversed later.
The report estimates that around 337 million children worldwide face riverine flooding, 662 million face tropical storms, 33 million are exposed to coastal flooding, approximately 1.2 billion experience extreme heat and nearly 1.8 billion face drought. Around 80% of children exposed to riverine and coastal flooding live in only 10 countries, with Bangladesh among the most heavily affected.
These global figures remind us that Bangladesh occupies the frontline of a worldwide crisis. Yet unlike wealthier nations, Bangladesh must confront this emergency while still addressing poverty, rapid urbanization, infrastructure deficits, and demographic pressures.
This makes policy choices especially important. Climate adaptation cannot remain concentrated only within environment ministries. It must become the organizing principle across education, public health, urban planning, and social protection.
A single national blueprint cannot adequately protect them all. Floating schools may be appropriate in flood-prone wetlands. Residential educational facilities may prove more effective in remote hill regions. Coastal districts require stronger shelter systems designed specifically around children’s needs. Urban schools increasingly need shaded environments capable of protecting students during prolonged heatwaves.
Climate adaptation succeeds only when geography shapes policy. Equally important is recognizing that children are not merely recipients of protection.
Young people increasingly understand climate risks because they experience them firsthand. Many already participate in community preparedness programs, environmental campaigns, and local adaptation initiatives. Their perspectives often reveal practical problems adults overlook.
Treating children solely as vulnerable populations ignores their potential as active participants in building resilience.
Unicef rightly argues that children should be meaningfully included in climate policy-making. This is not symbolic participation. It reflects the reality that today’s policy decisions will define their entire futures far more than they will affect current decision-makers.
There is also an uncomfortable issue the international community cannot continue avoiding. Bangladeshi children contribute almost nothing to global greenhouse gas emissions. Yet they bear some of the world’s highest climate risks.
This remains one of the greatest moral failures of modern international politics. The countries and populations least responsible for warming the planet continue paying its highest human costs. Climate justice therefore cannot remain confined to abstract diplomatic language during international summits. It must translate into predictable adaptation finance, technology transfer, and long-term investments focused specifically on children’s well-being.
HM Nazmul Alam is an Academic, Journalist, and Political Analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he teaches at IUBAT.

item.title: Trapped behind the scam
item.description:
In November last year, a young man named Abdullah Molla left Bangladesh for Cambodia, believing he had found a proper office job. What he found instead was captivity. He was pushed into an online scam compound, stripped of his documents, and held until his family, back home, borrowed heavily to buy his freedom.
Another Bangladeshi, Shafiqul Islam Hridoy, was promised $800 a month for data entry work. He was locked in a dark room for 17 days, beaten, and given electric shocks, because he refused to defraud strangers online.
According to the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, more than 300 Bangladeshis have already been rescued and repatriated from scam compounds in Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam, and elsewhere in Southeast Asia.
These are not distant tragedies. They are warnings written for Bangladesh, and we should read them carefully.
This year, the United Nations has chosen "Trapped Behind the Scam" as the theme for the World Day Against Trafficking in Persons. It is a deliberate shift in language.
For decades, the world pictured trafficking as physical movement into brothels, farms, or households. Today's traffickers have found a subtler and more profitable model: They recruit a person with a fake job advertisement, fly them across a border, take their passport, and force them to sit at a computer scamming other people, often for 18 hours a day, under threats of violence.
The United Nations Human Rights Office recently estimated that at least 300,000 people are held inside these scam compounds across the Mekong region alone, generating an estimated $64bn a year for organized crime. Interpol has confirmed that victims now come from at least 66 countries. Bangladesh is one of them.
Why this should worry us
It is tempting to treat this as someone else's crisis, a problem for Cambodia or Myanmar to solve. That comfort is misplaced. Bangladesh carries exactly the vulnerabilities that this new form of trafficking is built to exploit.
Consider the numbers. The Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics counted 1.94 million unemployed young people in its last full Labour Force Survey, and nearly a third of them held a university degree. An educated, underemployed, internet-literate youth population is not a liability by itself. But it is precisely the profile that scam recruiters look for, because fluent, tech-comfortable workers make more convincing scammers.
The same digital reach that lets a Dhaka graduate apply for a freelance job in London also lets a trafficker in Phnom Penh place a fraudulent advertisement on her Facebook feed. Add to this a well-worn migration culture, hundreds of thousands of Bangladeshis travel abroad for work every year, often through informal sub-agents rather than licensed recruiters, and the pathway from a hopeful jobseeker to a captive scammer becomes disturbingly short.
The US State Department's most recent Trafficking in Persons report on Bangladesh makes a further point worth sitting with: Traffickers are now using social media, mobile messaging, and artificial intelligence to identify and lure victims, particularly women and girls, with the same fluency that legitimate recruiters use to fill real vacancies. The tools of opportunity and the tools of exploitation have become almost indistinguishable.
A pattern Bangladesh already knows
None of this is entirely new to us. Bangladesh has long struggled with labour trafficking, child marriage-linked exploitation, domestic servitude, and cross-border trafficking involving the Rohingya population.
What online scam trafficking adds is a digital front door to an old house. The victim no longer needs to be poor, illiterate, or desperate in the ways we once assumed. She may have a smartphone, a degree, and a LinkedIn profile. That should unsettle our awareness campaigns, most of which still picture trafficking as something that happens to people with few choices, not people who believed they were making a smart one.
What Bangladesh has already done, and what is still missing
There is real progress to acknowledge. In a significant and timely step, Bangladesh has this year replaced its 2012 anti-trafficking law with the Human Trafficking and Migrant Smuggling Prevention and Suppression Act, 2026.
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed has described it as designed specifically to address crimes carried out through digital platforms and technology, a direct acknowledgement that our legal framework had fallen behind the criminals it was meant to stop.
The new law separates trafficking from migrant smuggling for the first time, strengthens investigation powers, allows the freezing of trafficking-linked assets, and enshrines the principle that a rescued victim should not be prosecuted as a criminal.
Alongside it, the judiciary has received a new Bench Book, developed with UNODC and the European Union, to help judges handle trafficking cases with the trauma-informed sensitivity these cases demand.
These are meaningful reforms. But laws only work when they are enforced, and enforcement in this space is unusually hard. Investigators need the capacity to trace cryptocurrency payments and follow evidence across borders. Diplomatic missions need faster channels to identify and repatriate victims held in remote compounds.
And crucially, our law enforcement and immigration officers need to be trained to recognize a rescued scam-centre worker as a trafficking victim first, not a cybercriminal. Abdullah Molla and Shafiqul Islam Hridoy were fortunate to come home. Many others, still trapped or too ashamed and indebted to seek help, are not.
A way forward
Protecting Bangladeshis from this crime does not require reinventing the wheel; it requires connecting pieces we already have.
Recruitment agencies and job platforms should be required to verify overseas postings before they are advertised. Bangladesh Bank and the Anti-Corruption Commission should be brought more closely into trafficking investigations, since this crime moves through financial systems as much as through borders.
Our missions abroad, particularly in Southeast Asia, need standing protocols for identifying and repatriating trafficking victims quickly. And our schools, universities, and job-training centres should teach a simple, urgent lesson: A job offer that asks you to hand over your passport, or that came from someone you have only ever met on Telegram, deserves suspicion before it deserves an air ticket.
Human trafficking no longer waits at the border. It arrives as a notification on a phone. If Bangladesh wants to protect the very opportunities that digital life offers our young people, our vigilance has to move online too, before more of our sons and daughters mistake a scam compound for a career.
Inmanuel Chayan Biswas, a humanitarian and development practitioner, is working for a prominent NGO in Bangladesh.

item.title: Winning the fight against trafficking
item.description:
Today is World Day Against Trafficking in Persons, and is a reminder that human trafficking remains one of the most persistent and damaging crimes. Every year, thousands of Bangladeshis fall victim to traffickers.
Yet, trafficking is no longer confined to borders, brokers, or physical coercion. Much of it has moved online, and we are now facing a new generation of threats that exploit digital technology, social media, and the vulnerabilities of young people seeking opportunity.
Human trafficking has always preyed on desperation. Today, it also preys on connectivity. Recruiters no longer need to visit villages or operate through local agents; they can reach victims through Facebook groups, messaging apps, job portals, and livestream platforms.
From false job offers to fraudulent migration schemes, the digital shift has made trafficking faster, harder to detect, and easier to disguise as legitimate opportunity.
For Bangladesh, this evolution is especially dangerous. Millions of young people are online, often without digital literacy or awareness of the risks. Migrant workers increasingly rely on social media for job information. Traffickers have adapted, and our protection systems must adapt with equal speed.
Bangladesh has made progress in combating traditional trafficking routes, strengthening laws, and improving rescue and rehabilitation. But the digital dimension remains under-addressed.
Law enforcement lacks specialized cyber‑trafficking units. Border and migration officials are not always trained to identify victims recruited online. And survivors often struggle to navigate the legal system when exploitation begins on a screen rather than at a border.
On this day, the message is clear: Strengthening protection means also strengthening digital vigilance. Traffickers are online and Bangladesh must be ready to meet them there. Trafficking has changed and our response must change with it. We cannot rely on old tools to fight a new threat.

item.title: Saving our tigers
item.description:
The revelation that Bangladesh has only 189 tigers left should be treated for what it is - a national tragedy.
The Royal Bengal Tiger is the most iconic species we have as a nation, it is quite literally the symbol of our natural heritage. That its numbers keep dwindling, and State Minister for Fisheries and Livestock Sultan Salauddin warning that the current situation is not sufficient to protect the species from extinction, is deeply concerning.
When tiger numbers continue to fall, it signals deeper ecological distress that cannot be ignored. Experts have long cautioned that habitat loss, rising salinity, human encroachment, poaching, and climate‑driven changes in the Sundarbans are eroding the conditions tigers need to survive. The latest numbers only confirm that these pressures are intensifying.
Conserving tigers should not be viewed as only about protecting a single species. It is about safeguarding the entire biodiversity of the Sundarbans - our most critical natural buffer against natural disasters such as cyclones and tidal surges.
Bangladesh has taken steps: Strengthening patrols, expanding camera‑trap monitoring, and improving community engagement. However, it is plain to see that the scale of the challenge demands more.
Conservation must be backed by sustained investment, scientific research, and strict enforcement against poaching and illegal resource extraction. The forest also needs better protection from industrial pressures, unregulated tourism, and climate impacts that are already reshaping its landscape.
We must also broaden our focus beyond tigers. Biodiversity loss has been accelerating nationwide, from wetlands to hill forests to coastal ecosystems. Protecting wildlife therefore requires a holistic strategy, from restoring habitats to regulating development to integrating conservation into national planning rather than treating it as an isolated sector.
The tiger population can recover, but only if we are able to act decisively, consistently, and with long‑term vision. Saving the tiger means saving the Sundarbans, and saving the Sundarbans means protecting our future.

item.title: Rajshahi boat capsize: Missing father, son's bodies recovered after two days
item.description:
The bodies of a father and his son, who had gone missing after a boat capsized in the Padma River in Rajshahi, were recovered two days after the accident, police said on Thursday.
The deceased were identified as Kawsar Ali, 60, the boatman, and his son Ziarul Haque, residents of Shyampur Shantinagar under Katakhali Police Station in Rajshahi.
Superintendent of Police (SP) of the Rajshahi Region River Police Mohammad Billal Hossain confirmed the recoveries.
According to police and Fire Service officials, divers from the Fire Service and River Police had been conducting a joint search operation since Tuesday's capsize. However, strong currents in the Padma River carried the bodies far from the accident site.
Kawsar Ali's body was recovered at around 8:00 am on Thursday after locals spotted it floating in the Padma River near Pakshi Bridge in Banglabazar, Kushtia, and alerted police.
Later, at around 1:00 pm, River Police recovered the body of his son Ziarul Haque from the Padma River near Satbaria Char in Rajshahi's Paba upazila. The bodies were subsequently handed over to their family members, police said.
The accident occurred on Tuesday afternoon when an engine-powered boat carrying eight passengers and a consignment of jhau (tamarisk) trees was travelling from Char Majardia to Lalon Shah Muktamancha. The vessel was overwhelmed by strong waves in the middle of the Padma River, lost control and capsized.
Local residents rescued six passengers alive shortly after the capsize, while boatman Kawsar Ali and his son, Ziarul Haque, remained missing. A joint search operation by Fire Service divers and River Police was launched immediately and ended with the recovery of their bodies on Thursday.

item.title: Minister: Proposed law to protect parents’ property rights
item.description:
The government is planning to amend the Transfer of Property Act to allow parents to retain lifetime possession and enjoyment of property even after transferring it to their children, Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Md Asaduzzaman said on Thursday.
He made the remarks at a memorandum of understanding (MoU) signing ceremony between the National Legal Aid Services Organisation and non-governmental organisations Brac and BLAST on legal aid at the Secretariat.
The proposed amendment aims to strengthen legal protection for parents who transfer property to their children but later become financially or socially vulnerable.
"We are considering an amendment to the relevant law because most civil cases in Bangladesh arise from disputes over property distribution and ownership," he said.
Under Muslim law, property can be transferred through heba (gift), while Hindu law recognises wills and Muslim law also provides for wills (wasiyat), he said.
However, once parents transfer property through heba, they immediately lose ownership and often become dependent on their children, he said adding: "If children do not look after their parents, the parents are left with little legal protection and become helpless.”
To address the issue, the government plans to expand provisions under the Transfer of Property Act relating to gifts, drawing on a 1963 judgment of the Pakistan Supreme Court.
Under the proposed amendment, a parent transferring property as a gift would retain a usufruct right, allowing them to possess and enjoy the property throughout their lifetime.
"A parent may choose not to transfer property through heba or a will, but instead make a gift while continuing to enjoy and occupy the property during his or her lifetime," he said.
Under the proposal, although ownership would be transferred, the parents would retain lifetime possession. Neither the parents nor the children would be able to sell the property unilaterally.
Any sale by the parents would require the children's consent, while the children would also need the parents' permission to dispose of the property during the parents' lifetime, said the minister.
Asaduzzaman said provisions would also be included for exceptional circumstances, such as when a parent requires urgent medical treatment and the property must be sold but the children refuse consent.
"In such cases, the district judge will be empowered to consider an application and decide whether the sale should be allowed," he said.
The law minister expressed hope that the proposed reform would help reduce property-related civil litigation and resolve many disputes through clearer legal safeguards.
"We believe this initiative will reduce the number of civil cases in future and address many existing problems. We want to move forward with such new legal ideas," he added.

item.title: Rushdie assailant convicted of terrorism charges
item.description:
A federal jury on Wednesday convicted novelist Salman Rushdie’s assailant of “engaging in an act of terrorism” for the bloody August 2022 attack at a New York cultural center.
Hadi Matar, a 28-year-old Lebanese American, “chose to align his values with the terroristic values of the leaders of Iran,” said US Attorney Michael DiGiacomo, adding the defendant spent months planning the stabbing that nearly killed Rushdie and left him blind in one eye.
Matar was also convicted of supporting the Iran-backed Lebanese militant group Hezbollah, after investigators found materials from the organization at his home.
Federal prosecutors said Matar followed a fatwa calling for Rushdie’s execution, first issued in 1989 by the late Iranian leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, for fictionalizing the Prophet Muhammad in his bestselling book, “The Satanic Verses.”
The fatwa was reaffirmed in 2017 by Iran’s late Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, and endorsed in a 2006 speech by Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah, prosecutors said.
“His brutal attack on Mr. Rushdie during a peaceful speaking event is a chilling reminder of the global reach of Iranian terrorism,” DiGiacomo said.
Rushdie testified during Matar’s federal trial last week, speaking in court for nearly an hour about the assault.
When asked if he believed Matar was motivated to carry out the fatwa, Rushdie replied: “I had no knowledge of that. I have my suspicions,” according to US media.
The attack took place at the Chautauqua Institution in Mayville, New York, during a free speech conference, where then-24-year-old Matar leapt onto the stage and stabbed Rushdie repeatedly with a six-inch blade.
In 2024, Rushdie published a memoir recounting the near-death experience called “Knife,” in which he has an imagined conversation with Matar.
A documentary about the assault, titled “Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie,” premiered at the Sundance Film Festival earlier this year.
Matar was already convicted of attempted murder and sentenced to 25 years in prison by the New York state justice system, and now faces an additional maximum federal penalty of life in prison.
He is due for sentencing Nov. 3, though the New York Times reported Matar’s attorney, Nathaniel Barone II, said he intended to appeal the ruling.
Matar told a reporter before his trials that he believed Rushdie had “attacked Islam.”
Rushdie lived in seclusion in London for a decade after the 1989 fatwa, but for the past 20 years -- until the attack -- lived relatively normally in New York.
In 2026, Rushdie said violence is the tool of “the unscrupulous using the ignorant” to attack culture.
“For the authoritarian, culture is the enemy. Whether that’s journalism or universities or music or writing,” Rushdie said. “The uncultured and ignorant, and the radical don’t like it, and they take steps against it, which we see every day.”

item.title: May, June heatwaves caused 2,877 extra deaths in England
item.description:
Record-breaking heatwaves in May and June led to an estimated 2,877 excess deaths in England, the UK Health Security Agency said Wednesday.
The provisional figure is almost double the total for the whole of the summer in 2025, which was 1,504, and represents “a substantial public health impact,” the Ukhsa government agency said.
“These figures highlight the significant danger that very hot weather can pose to people’s health,” said Ross Thompson, principal environmental public health scientist at the Ukhsa.
Health minister Yvette Cooper said the United Kingdom is accustomed to higher rates of illness in winter, but “now we are seeing the summer heat have an increasingly serious impact on the health of thousands of people.”
The latest figure does not take into account the current month of July, which has also seen a prolonged heatwave, and the Ukhsa said the total for the summer “is likely to be substantially higher.”
“Based on the interim data, it is likely that 2026 could see the highest number of heat-associated deaths on record,” it said.
The excess mortality figure is calculated by comparing the average number of deaths on days when the temperature exceeds 20°C with the average number on cooler days.
In May there were 753 extra deaths and in June, when there was a rare red heat warning, there were 2,124.
The Uksha stressed the need for communities and services to prepare for hot weather from the start of summer rather than just at its height.
The record mortality figure for a whole summer was set in 2022, when 2,985 deaths associated with heat were recorded.
The Climate Change Committee (CCC), the body responsible for advising the government on climate change, warned last year the UK was “not ready” to deal with the consequences of climate change.
In a report published in May, it estimated 92% of British homes could be too hot by 2050, and recommended the government set maximum temperature limits in the workplace, as well as investing in air conditioning for public buildings such as hospitals and schools.

item.title: Deaths in Ukraine after Zelensky warns of Russian strikes
item.description:
At least eight people were killed in Ukraine overnight as Russia said it conducted airstrikes on targets across the country.
One person was killed in an airstrike on Kyiv, the capital of Ukraine, while other fatalities were reported as far west as Lviv.
Explosions were reported over Kyiv in the early hours of Thursday after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Russia might conduct a “massive attack.”
Zelensky later wrote that Russia had fired 70 rockets and 280 drones in the attack.
Both Reuters and AFP cited people on the ground as saying they had heard explosions.
“Sadly, one death has been confirmed,” the Kyiv city military administration wrote on Telegram in the early hours of Thursday.
Russia struck Kyiv with ballistic missiles, the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said, urging people to seek shelter. He added that several nonresidential sites in Kyiv caught fire.
“The enemy is attacking the capital with ballistic weapons. The threat of further attack remains present. Stay in shelters!” Klitschko said.
Russia also attacked other Ukrainian cities overnight. At least six people, including two girls, were killed in a Russian missile strike on the central Ukrainian city of Kryvyi Rih, according to the head of the local military administration.
“In a village on the outskirts of Kryvyi Rih, a direct strike by an Iskander-M ballistic missile, launched from Voronezh, hit a private house where a large family lived, killing girls aged five and 12 and four adults,” Oleksandr Vilkul said.
He added that eight more people were wounded and that the death toll could rise..
Russian missiles also damaged two apartment buildings and injured six people in Lviv, a city in western Ukraine near the Polish border, according to local officials.
Meanwhile, the Polish Armed Forces announced on X that Poland had scrambled its fighter jets on Thursday to protect its airspace amid Russian airstrikes on Ukraine.
“Fighter aircraft and an early warning aircraft have begun operations while ground-based air defense systems and radar reconnaissance systems have reached a state of readiness,” the post said, adding that the actions are preventive in nature.
The strikes came after Zelensky warned of a “high probability that the strike will be carried out tonight.”
“I received a report from Air Force Commander Anatolii Kryvonozhko. The Russians prepared a massive attack several days ago,” Zelensky said on X.
The Ukrainian president stressed that Ukrainians’ safety depended on the willingness of Kyiv’s allies to provide anti-missile defenses. His statements came on the heels of a trip to the US, where he said President Donald Trump had agreed to give Ukraine licenses related to Patriot missile production.
Zelensky said Thursday: “It is important that our partners fully understand what’s happening, and that the protection of lives directly depends on their readiness, or lack thereof, to help us with air defense missiles.”
For its part, Ukraine continued its attacks on logistics centers inside Russia on Thursday.
In Penza, a warehouse belonging to online retailer Wildberries, often referred to as Russia’s Amazon, caught fire after being struck by a Ukrainian drone, injuring one person and triggering the evacuation of 200 others.
Ukraine says Wildberries is providing logistical support for Russia’s military.
Its attacks inside Russia also target the country’s already anemic domestic economy and drive home to ordinary Russians the message that the war is not simply something that affects Ukrainians.

item.title: Experts: Concerted efforts can unlock cotton cultivation’s true potential in Bangladesh
item.description:
Experts have called for coordinated action to expand cotton cultivation in Bangladesh, highlighting its potential as a climate-adaptive and economically viable crop.
They noted that although Bangladesh is the world's second-largest exporter of ready-made garments, around 97% of the cotton used by the country's textile industry is imported, costing the country more than $3 billion annually.
These observations were made at the National Dialogue on Cotton: Its Future Opportunities as a Climate Adaptive Crop, organized by BRAC's Climate and Environmental Innovation Program (CEIP) at the Brac Centre in Mohakhali, Dhaka, on Thursday, July 30.
The dialogue examined the structural barriers to expanding domestic cotton production and explored practical measures relating to policy, research, financing, agricultural extension services, market development, and post-harvest management.
Md Rezaul Amin, executive director (routine duties) of the Cotton Development Board, said that cotton is a beneficial crop from multiple perspectives. In addition to increasing farmers' incomes, cotton cultivation can contribute to climate change adaptation and generate employment opportunities across the value chain.
He added that the government is providing incentives to encourage farmers to cultivate cotton.
Md Liakath Ali, director of Brac's Climate and Environmental Innovation Program (CEIP) and Disaster Risk Management Program (DRMP), said that cotton offers a promising alternative in areas where agricultural production has been affected by climate change.
He emphasized expanding cotton cultivation across the country would require close collaboration among government agencies, the private sector, development organizations, and other stakeholders.
M Farid Uddin, senior agronomic adviser/consultant at CottonConnect South Asia Private Limited and former executive director of the Cotton Development Board, said that Bangladesh currently cultivates cotton on approximately 45,000 hectares of land, producing an estimated 200,000 bales annually (each bale weighing 220 kilograms), meeting only around 2% of national demand.
He also noted that cotton is a carbon-positive crop and that the government officially declared cotton an agricultural commodity one year ago.
Among those attending the event was Mitali Chakma , a cotton farmer from Manikchhari in Rangamati.
She said: "I received seeds and training from the Cotton Development Board. I have been cultivating cotton for the past three years. There is considerable interest in cotton cultivation among farmers. With the necessary support, cotton cultivation can expand significantly across the Chattogram Hill Tracts."
Participants observed that the challenges facing cotton production extend beyond cultivation itself. Cotton competes with rice, tobacco, and high-value winter vegetables for agricultural land.
Harvesting remains largely manual, while farmers continue to face constraints in accessing finance, agricultural inputs, extension services, storage facilities, ginning services, and reliable markets.
The discussion also highlighted the significant potential for cotton cultivation in climate-vulnerable regions, including the Barind Tract, coastal saline areas, riverine chars, and the Chattogram Hill Tracts.
As a heat- and drought-tolerant crop, cotton requires less water than rice, making it a suitable option for climate adaptation and livelihood diversification.
Participants also noted that replacing tobacco cultivation with cotton in selected regions could provide farmers with a more sustainable alternative.
The dialogue opened with remarks by Abu Sadat Moniruzzaman Khan, program head, Climate and Environmental Innovation Program (CEIP), Brac.
Other speakers included Abed Chaudhury, independent agro-specialist; Md Kutub Uddin, deputy director (HQ), Cotton Development Board; Md Manirul Islam, additional director (cash crop), Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE); and Prof Mohammad Kamrul Hasan, Professor (Department of Agroforestry), Bangladesh Agricultural University.
Representatives from Bangladesh Agricultural Research Council (BARC), Bangladesh Agricultural University (BAU), Bank Asia, Primark, WeGro, and other organizations also participated in the dialogue.

item.title: Industries demand policy for publishing microplastic research
item.description:
Representatives from the country’s leading industrial enterprises have demanded that private organizations inform the relevant regulatory body and allow an opportunity for verification before publishing research reports on the presence of microplastics or other harmful elements in consumer goods, including toothpaste.
At the same time, they called for the formulation of a clear law or policy regarding the publication of such research reports.
Speakers raised these demands on Thursday during a public hearing organized at the BSTI (Bangladesh Standards and Testing Institution) headquarters in Tejgaon, Dhaka.
The chief guest of the event was BSTI director general (secretary) Kazi Imdadul Hoque.
Joint secretary for industries Md Saiful Islam, attended as special guest.
The event was presided over by BSTI director (administration) Md Saiful Islam.
Speaking at the public hearing, BSTI director general Kazi Imdadul Hoque said that BSTI evaluates every research study seriously and emphasized the need for quality research in the country.
However, he noted that research findings should not be published in a manner that creates unnecessary panic or confusion among the public. He added that if BSTI, as the regulatory body, had been informed before the results of the research on microplastics in toothpaste were published, it would have been more coordinated and acceptable.
He further stated that there is currently no reason to panic regarding the presence of microplastics in toothpaste, as no recognized global standard has established an acceptable limit for this element.
BSTI's relevant expert committee will review international standards, including those of the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), to take the necessary decisions on this matter.
Representatives from industrial enterprises argued that there is no guarantee that research conducted by a private entity always follows internationally recognized methods. Therefore, reviewing or verifying the findings with regulatory bodies prior to publication would help avoid confusion.
Md Sohel Hossain, senior legal counsel in the legal and regulatory affairs department at Square Group, noted that toothpaste is a product covered under BSTI's mandatory quality certification. Consequently, discussions with BSTI should have taken place before publishing the results of such research. This would have provided an opportunity to verify the actual facts and avoid unnecessary confusion and financial losses for businesses.
Citing a recent incident, Md Shafiqur Rahman Bhuiyan, international marketing adviser at Olympic Industries, pointed out that although claims were made regarding the presence of potassium bromate in several bakery products, subsequent testing by BSTI and the Bangladesh Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (BCSIR) found no trace of the chemical.
However, prior to that, negative publicity had already caused irreparable damage to the reputation and business of the company concerned.
Speakers stated that publishing incomplete or unverified research leads to negative publicity or "media trials" across news outlets and social media platforms. This misleads consumers while damaging company market positions and reputations.
Several proposals were also raised during the public hearing aimed at making BSTI services simpler and more business-friendly.
These included launching an online payment system, providing options to submit all applications and required documents online, accepting online renewal applications alongside new license requests, formulating a Bangladesh standard for growing-up milk for children aged 3 to 5 years, and updating specific clauses of packaged commodities laws and regulations.
Representatives from various industrial enterprises attended the event, including Square Food & Beverage, Pran-RFL Group, Nestlé Bangladesh, Bangladesh Edible Oil, Transcom Consumer Products, Akij Resource, New Zealand Dairy Bangladesh, ACI Food & Beverage, Unilever Bangladesh, Marico Bangladesh, Meghna Group, Reckitt Benckiser, Arla Foods Bangladesh, IFAD Group, Nabisco Biscuit, and Mega Group of Industries.

item.title: EBL and bKash jointly introduce FDR on bKash App
item.description:
Eastern Bank PLC (EBL) and bKash jointly introduced the country's first digital FDR (Fixed Deposit) available on bKash App, marking a significant milestone in advancing financial inclusion.
bKash users can now instantly open FDR from bKash App, without visiting branches or submitting paper documents.
By making reliable savings products more accessible, the initiative aims to help people across the country, including those in semi-urban and rural areas, grow their savings conveniently with one of the leading banks in Bangladesh.
bKash customers can now open FDR with EBL ranging from Tk10,000 to Tk100,000 having tenures of 6 and 12 months, with auto-renewal option.
Customers will receive periodic interest in bKash account.
Besides, customers can download and preserve digital receipts from bKash app.
M Khorshed Anowar, deputy managing director and head of retail and SME banking at EBL and Ali Ahmmed, chief commercial officer of bKash Limited, jointly made the announcement at an event held at EBL Head Office in the city on July 29.
Other senior officials from both the organizations were also present at the event.
M Khorshed Anowar, DMD of EBL, said: “After the successful launch of EBL DPS in bKash App, we took the initiative to be the first bank to offer Fixed Deposit in bKash App. This a testament to the inclusive banking EBL is striving for. Now people across Bangladesh can open EBL Fixed Deposit as per their convenience on bKash App. EBL will continue to extend its savings services to a broader customer segment as a way forward to inclusive banking.”
Ali Ahmmed, chief commercial officer of bKash, said: “The deeper collaboration between banks and bKash is creating new opportunities to deliver accessible, innovative, and customer-centric financial solutions for the entire country. By leveraging bKash’s extensive customer base and digital infrastructure, banks can extend their services to millions with greater convenience. Through this partnership, we have further expanded our common objectives of innovating financial products supporting financial inclusion and empowerment.”

item.title: Prime Bank holds ‘Empowering Youth Season 2.0’ session at UIU
item.description:
Prime Bank PLC. held another session of its flagship “Empowering Youth–Season 2.0” initiative at United International University (UIU), bringing together industry leaders and aspiring graduates to bridge the gap between academia and the corporate world.
Rup Ratan Pine, executive director (grade-I) of Bangladesh Bank, attended the session as chief guest.
Addressing the students, he underscored the importance of academic results as well as extracurricular involvement in securing strong career opportunities in both government and private sectors, including prospects at Bangladesh Bank.
He also encouraged students to take advantage of Bangladesh Bank’s Student Banking facility to build sound financial literacy and savings habits early on, laying the groundwork for long-term financial stability and independence.
M Nazeem A Choudhury, additional managing director and head of consumer & SME banking division at Prime Bank PLC, delivered the keynote speech on employability and the essential skill sets needed to thrive in today’s competitive job market.
Drawing from his own career journey, he shared candid reflections on the challenges he faced and the critical decisions that shaped his path — offering students a rare, real-world perspective on how resilience and sound judgment can turn obstacles into stepping stones toward leadership.
MM Mahbub Hasan, senior vice president and head of financial inclusion & school banking at Prime Bank, spoke about the bank’s 31-year journey of credible milestones, including its distinctive academic initiative, PrimeAcademia.
He also emphasized the importance of financial inclusion and sound money management for students as they prepare to enter the workforce.
The program was chaired by Prof Md Abul Kashem Mia, vice chancellor of United International University, while Prof Salma Karim, director of the BBA Program at UIU, delivered the welcome address.
Speaking to the students, the panel highlighted the growing importance of innovation, financial literacy, digital transformation, and continuous learning in shaping the future of Bangladesh’s banking industry.
They also urged participants to build strong professional competencies and embrace ethical leadership as they chart their career paths.
The session concluded with an interactive Q&A, giving students the opportunity to engage directly with industry experts on career development and the banking profession.
A live mock interview session was also organized, offering participants hands-on interview experience, constructive feedback, and valuable insight into corporate recruitment practices.
Through its “Empowering Youth” initiative, Prime Bank continues to strengthen industry-academia collaboration, equipping young talents with practical knowledge, career guidance, and financial literacy awareness- reaffirming its commitment to nurturing the next generation of skilled professionals in Bangladesh.

item.title: Hossain Zillur Rahman: Key to change lies in the hands of citizens
item.description:
A public lecture titled ‘What Drives Change: Today’s Questions’ was held on Thursday, July 30, at the 'Manzur Elahi' Auditorium of East West University.
Eminent economist and chairman of Brac Hossain Zillur Rahman delivered the keynote address.
In his speech, Rahman outlined six drivers of change: narrative, institution, norms, initiatives, power, and interest groups.
He highlighted how both the positive and negative aspects of these drivers impact the nation's economy.
Rahman emphasized that Bangladesh must move away from a cheap-labor-dependent economy that relies primarily on garments and remittances.
He noted that the country has struggled to embody democratic principles in state practices and has been unable to fully capitalize on its demographic dividend, leaving the economy stagnant.
To achieve positive change, he urged a focus on several key areas, including reforming the concept of the state to view it as a service to the people rather than as an entity above them.
He also called for addressing the lack of professionalism among local professionals, improving the quality of education with forward-looking foresight, and shifting social norms toward greater cleanliness and transparency.
Drawing historical parallels to 1947, 1971, and 2024, Dr. Rahman remarked that the persistent aspiration for change among the citizens of Bangladesh is the nation's greatest strength. In times of national crisis, citizen-led innovation and grassroots initiatives have consistently paved the path toward solutions.
Therefore, he concluded, the ultimate key to change lies in the hands of the citizens.
Presiding over the event, Prof Mohammed Farashuddin, chairperson of the board of trustees of East West University, highlighted that the benefits of national development are failing to reach the vulnerable and voiceless segments of society.
He called for special attention to healthcare and education for underprivileged populations and urged action to address the growing deficit of social equity.
Earlier, Prof Shams Rahman, vice chancellor of East West University, delivered the welcome address.
Members of the board of trustees, faculty members, students, officers, and staff of the university were present at the event.

item.title: Directorate of Posts gets Tk18.5cr revenue share from Nagad for FY26
item.description:
Mobile financial service (MFS) provider Nagad has handed over Tk18.56 crore to the Directorate of Posts as its revenue share for FY26, marking a 34% year-on-year increase.
The revenue share grew by over Tk5 crore compared to the figure in the previous fiscal year.
Bangladesh Bank-appointed Administrator for Nagad, Md Motasem Billah, handed over the cheque to Minister for Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology Fakir Mahbub Anam, MP, at a ceremony at Daak Bhaban in the capital’s Agargaon Wednesday.
Posts and Telecommunications Secretary Bilquis Jahan Rimi, Director General of the Directorate of Posts Kazi Asadul Islam and senior officials from both organisations were present.
Minister for Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology Fakir Mahbub Anam said: “Without Nagad, there will be a monopoly in the market, and we will not allow that to happen. Nagad must maintain a competitive market and become even more profitable.”
Calling on journalists present at the event not to heed any rumours regarding Nagad, the minister said there is no alternative to digital transactions for the development of people in remote areas, students, and general people.
​“People know Nagad is a state-backed institution. Therefore, we must move forward with Nagad through essential activities and services,” he added.
Posts and Telecommunications Secretary Bilkis Jahan Rimi said: “Today is a day of joy for us. The government has earned a substantial amount of revenue through Nagad. We will work on exploring further avenues for the Directorate of Posts to collaborate with Nagad.”
Director General of the Directorate of Posts Kazi Asadul Islam said: “We often hear that state-owned entities cannot turn a profit, but we have disproven that narrative through Nagad and demonstrated that government services can indeed be profitable.”
​Highlighting the operator’s financial contribution since its inception, the director general noted that Nagad has so far paid Tk946 crore in taxes to the government alongside Tk47 crore in revenue shares to the postal department.
​“In total, the government has received nearly Tk1,000 crore since Nagad’s inception, which is a significant achievement. Building on the trust and goodwill of marginalised people, we aim to move further forward in the days ahead,” he added.
Nagad Administrator Md Motasem Billah said Nagad has made an outstanding contribution to bringing marginalised people across the country under financial inclusion through technology.
“Besides driving innovations, Nagad plays the paramount role in safeguarding consumer interests by enhancing market competition. At the same time, the operator continues to play a vital role in generating revenue for the government every year,” he added.
Currently, the company records a daily average transaction volume exceeding Tk1,500 crore.
As per the partnership agreement, Nagad Limited bears all capital and operational expenditures, including technological infrastructure, requiring no financial investment from the postal department.
Following the deduction of specific allowable operational expenses from total revenue, the Directorate of Posts receives 51% of the net proceeds, while Nagad Limited retains the remaining 49%.
Before this latest payment, Nagad Limited had disbursed nearly Tk28.5 crore in cumulative revenue shares to the Postal Department since its inception.
With the addition of the disbursement for the recently concluded FY26, Nagad’s total revenue contribution to the Directorate of Posts stands at Tk47 crore.
Earlier in March 2026, Nagad handed over Tk13.82 crore for the 18 months spanning January 2024 to June 2025.
Previous disbursements included Tk5.51 crore in 2024 and Tk4.50 crore in 2022. Over the preceding years, Nagad provided Tk4.5 crore in revenue share to the postal department.
Beyond this, the MFS operator paid Tk313 crore to the exchequer in VAT and other taxes during the first 11 months of the current fiscal year.
In FY26, Nagad processed transactions totalling Tk427,000 crore – a 25.5% year-on-year growth from Tk340,000 crore in the preceding year.
Alongside the steady surge in transaction volume and count, the operator’s user base expanded substantially, with active customers surpassing 30 million as of June, including over 22.5 million app users.
